utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today is Wednesday, the 18th of March, 2009. I greet the accused and their counsels. Mr. Stringer and all his colleagues. As well as Mr. Usher and all the people who assist us in the courtroom. I think that Mr. Registrar as an IC number to give us, I give him the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution has submitted its response to Stojic Defence objection to the Prosecution's list of documents tendered through witness Hamid Bahto, this list shall be given IC954. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Ms. Alaburic, you have the floor. I think you have a bit more than 20 minutes left. 23 minutes to be precise, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Cross-examination Ms. Alaburic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bandic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to all in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bandic, let us try to use these 20-odd minutes to show as many relevant details as possible to Their Honours. Yesterday we were dealing with document P4699.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be given the binder with my documents. I would kindly ask the usher for his assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the meantime we can focus on screens. 4699 is the document that we are dealing with, page 18 in Croatian, which corresponds to page 11 and then 12 in the English text. In this big binder -- oh, I'm sorry, yes, it's a separate document. Right. So page 18. You don't have to look at it yet because I'm going to put a very general question to you. We said yesterday that the authorities of Herceg-Bosna wanted to create the HVO as a multiethnic army of both the Croats and the Muslims who live in the territory Herceg-Bosna and in the other areas where the HVO was fighting against the Serb forces; is that right, Mr. Bandic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Bandic, as for what we saw here, the attack on Bioelo Brdo and the area north of Mostar, what happened on the 30th of June, do you know of any other example of a Muslim citizen who was a soldier of the HVO who would have been disarmed, mistreated, detained, dismissed from the army because he was a Muslim? Do you know of any other such case?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, madam counsellor, good morning to all. In relation to your question, I can say that I am not aware of any case when persons of Muslim ethnicity were mistreated on account of that in any way. There were many ethnic Muslims or, rather, Bosniaks later, who were members of the HVO. If you allow me, I would just like to say a few words in relation to this specific case because this has to do with a survey up until mid-1993 by when, regrettably, there had been some incidents. In April, I think, that year, we learned certain things and we obtained the documents of the commander of the corps in Mostar, Mr. Pasalic, where he speaks about our people in the HVO. Of course, the reference is being made to ethnic Muslims, Bosniaks, and he is counting on them in the attack. So we had some indicia that this might happen and that persons of Bosniak ethnicity who were within the HVO could be used. I remember that very well. When Mr. Lucic, or rather, when we were dealing with this report and trying to define things as specifically as possible, we did have certain indicia to the effect that on the basis of political developments as well, because at the time Mr. Hadziosmanovic had been replaced. I personally happen to know Mr. Hadziosmanovic, he was a very moderate person who headed the SDA, and that was the point when he and some other moderates in the SDA were dismissed. So quite simply it was the policy of the SDA that was changing, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A sub-question, you mentioned the documentation and plans of Mr. Arif Pasalic and the army Bosnia-Hercegovina headquartered in Mostar. Tell me, do you know that very similar plans were in the Bregava Brigade, and they had plans to take Stolac together with the Muslims in HVO?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I have an objection. I recognise the Trial Chamber has given counsel additional time to conduct this examination. I'd suggest that this line of questioning is outside the scope of the direct examination, and therefore that counsel should not be allowed to ask leading questions during this part. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I just respond. During the direct examination, the witness was giving answers about Dretelj, Gabela, Heliodrom, and other detention centres and, generally speaking, about measures that were being taken. My current questions are directly related to these detention centres because the majority of the persons who were detained in Dretelj, Gabela, and the Heliodrom were precisely HVO soldiers who were of Muslim ethnicity. So I think that this is directly related to the examination-in-chief. Of course, if the Honourable Trial Chamber rules otherwise, I will fully abide by your ruling, and there's no need for me to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Ms. Alaburic, the Chamber has deliberated and feels that during the examination-in-chief, the questions dealing with the conditions in which people were detained and not why they were detained, we feel that there is no need to ask those questions. So we will ask you to proceed and move on to another topic. Yes, or please do not ask leading questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to deal with a direct link with the examination-in-chief. Mr. Bandic, if I observed correctly, you said during your examination-in-chief that in the detention centres about which you were asked there were civilians actually?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know that in these centres, there were Muslim soldiers of the HVO who had been disarmed in the beginning of July 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And a large number at that. For the most part actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's deal with the reports because I have a few more topics that I would like us to discuss. In the next section of this report, there is a reference to SIS activities in registering and processing a series of crimes. Yesterday, we talked about that. We talked about the line of work of the SIS; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In this same section it says, It is necessary to point out that in relation to that, a special contribution was given by the SIS centre in Vitez and there is some documentation in this regard. I conclude on the basis of this sentence that SIS centres had a direct responsibility to deal with uncovering and prosecuting perpetrators of crimes; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, madam, that is partly correct. If we say the SIS centre -- if you allow me, the SIS centre in Vitez, that practically never started to function, as you've seen, due to objective and subjective reasons. There was a total of five persons there, and we believed that they belonged to the SIS centre. However, in the field that is the task that they had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We will be dealing with central Bosnia separately. Already on the next document, the next document is P7419, the very next one. That is a report for the second half of 1993. We are just going to analyse one particular section. On a page that has ERN number 409. It's page 3, actually, in that document.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, could you please help me out with this. Where is this?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the big binder. The last document in the fourth section. But you have it on the screen now. We are just dealing with one particular section. That's right. I'm saying for Their Honours that it is the fifth paragraph on page 2. Mr. Bandic, on the basis of the situation in the administration of SIS, there was a new organisation of the SIS centre and the SIS in HVO units. The sentence I want is the following: "New conditions were created for the SIS to be in the function of the units of the HVO." I'll try to deal with this as briefly as possible. The new establishment of the SIS towards the end of 1993 was initiated and realised by Mr. Ljubica as the minister and Mr. Biskic as -- as the assistant for security. I'm stopping for the sake of the transcript. Towards the end of 1993 Mr. Jukic -- as the new minister of defence and Mr. Jukic as his security assistant. Can you explain to us, Mr. Bandic what does that mean? That it was only this new establishment of the SIS that was supposed to make it possible for the SIS to be in the function of the units of the HVO. I infer on this basis that the establishment until then was not in that function?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Alaburic, Your Honours, Ms. Alaburic, you see we are dealing with the end of 1993, along with all these terrible problems that we were dealing with for a year and a half. This is a moment when there were major changes, politically and from a military point of view and from a personnel point of view. In the military and in the political sections, respectively. Please don't hold this against me, the fact that I'm dealing with this matter at such length, but this led to a recapitulation of the situation in the entire HVO including the area that we are discussing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bandic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we just interrupt your answer, I do apologise for the interruption. We will deal with this re-organisation in relation to SIS centres precisely dealing with the example of central Bosnia, if we have enough time. But before that I would like us to discuss Stupni Do a bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours my first document is going to be a document that is under seal. I am going to be referring to statements made by a protected witness, so I believe that at first in order to be as cautious as possible that we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the last paragraph --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session for the record. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is said, Mr. Bandic, that General Blaskic said that in June, 1993, a new problem arose in the parallel chain of command by the establishment of the SIS centre at Vitez and that new organisation was not in any connection with the operation zone and functioned independent from the SIS assistant of the operative zone. Tell us, did you know about that as being a problem and the opinion of Mr. Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was known to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the first part of this report it is said that as late as the beginning of 1994, a re-organisation was carried out by disbanding certain special purpose unit and by establishing Guards Brigades, and only then Mr. Blaskic had full control over units in the area of central Bosnia. Please tell us, was this thesis of General Blaskic known to you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was known to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next document, 4D1320, another report from the Blaskic trial, I'm interested in a part of a sentence in the sixth paragraph, it's very short, before it appears on the screen I will read it out loud, And parts of the proofs illustrate the existence of parallel lines of command over special purpose units which led Grude and Mostar; in other words, to the leading people of Herceg-Bosna, Dario Kordic and Ignac Kostroman, which bypassed Blaskic. Please tell us, Mr. Bandic, whether you know anything about this thesis by General Blaskic that there was a parallel line of command which bypassed him?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is known to me this thesis, but Mr. Kostroman and Kordic were there in central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine, I will show you another article from Globus magazine entitled --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your time is up already, Ms. Alaburic, so this will be your last question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not a thesis of General Petkovic Defence, but I must stress that, first of all --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- but I would like to ask you about the thesis about special purpose units in Herceg-Bosna being under special influence of Bruno Stojic. My question is, and I repeat this is not General Petkovic thesis, but tell us, Mr. Bandic, that -- whether you know that this was a thesis of General Blaskic's Defence and Ante Nobilo Mr. Blaskic 's Defence counsel, still maintains that the second line of command emanated from the Ministry of Defence of the HZ HB; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam counsel, this is one of the many thesis. It's very arbitrary. It is known to me because I read it in the media.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since my time is out, I would like to conclude my cross-examination. Thank you for my extra time and thank you, Mr. Bandic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Interpretation] If you allow me, concerning the last question of my learned friend, that question was absolutely irrelevant and this question illustrates exactly what we've been maintaining all along, when it came to giving extra time is that Madam Alaburic in this courtroom is trying to indict Mr. Bruno Stojic. She is trying to indict Mr. Bruno Stojic, although she has been maintaining all along that she had been provoked by the Defence of Bruno Stojic. This is a very nasty business, and this is why I have to speak into the transcript. THE ACCUSED STOJIC: [Interpreted] I apologise. Good morning, Your Honours. I apologise, but this makes no sense. This was not the topic of examination-in-chief. If I knew that General Petkovic Defence would be putting forward this thesis, I would have brought hundreds of documents to prove that Blaskic was in charge and controlled the Vitezovi. I would have put this into 65 ter list, but I never knew that she would -- Madam Alaburic would raise such issues. She's constantly attacking my Defence team. You have to control this process, Your Honours. You gave her two hours extra and then ten minutes on top of that, this makes really no sense. You know what this means in the public opinion down there, that Bruno Stojic is attacking the Main Staff and this is not true. Please protect me from her in this courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stojic, you know that you are accused, you know that you are being defended by lawyers that support your Defence, you know that Mr. Petkovic via his counsel Ms. Alaburic is putting forward the theory of a double chain of command. Since they will call their own witnesses and when these witnesses will come, you will then have the opportunity to cross-examine these witnesses and challenge their submissions, and the bench will accord this the appropriate weight. Maybe you are right as far as Ms. Alaburic is concerned. Admittedly, Ms. Alaburic has been granted some time and during that time she puts her theory forward. Of course, this needs to be substantiated by documents. This is what I wanted to tell you, Mr. Stojic. Believe me, Mr. Stojic, we listen to what is being said in the courtroom, and we will weigh this at the end of the trial. Ms. Alaburic is putting a question to the witness, the witness answered the question, and that is where we stand now. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I never foresaw the need to clarify this point, and this is why I'm going to additionally clarify my -- what I just said. This is not General Petkovic thesis or Defence case. Mr. Petkovic testified in the Blaskic case and very clearly explained how things were. The issue of General Blaskic was structured in such a way to illustrate the reason for the conflict with General Blaskic and that the whole examination in the case of Blaskic to be put into context in the right and the proper way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before you -- I'm not going to get involved in a speech on this issue, but my intervention as far as its relevant is all questions, of course, must be relevant, and we didn't stand before to make objections. Your Honours had, of course, granted additional time, and Your Honours will make a determination if that time is needed and was actually merited after hearing the nature and focus of the cross-examination. But, Your Honours, one question right at the end stood out as completely outlandish in my respectful submission. The view as to what Mr. Nobilo may or may not have of the evidence is complete and utterly -- completely and utterly irrelevant. Your Honours, those that have practiced in these courts perhaps have seen Mr. Nobilo, I know my learned friend Mr. Stringer, who was involved in the Blaskic case, knows him to some extent. But whether or not he has particular views, whether they are cogent, coherent, whether they're the product of a diligent and proper investigation or whether they're not are completely irrelevant as a matter of cross-examination. Counsel on any party may have a whole variety of views from sober, very diligent, and well based views to actually outlandish theories, but they're hardly properly the matters of a diligent and proper cross-examination in my respectful submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to say something. No -- please, please, I also -- I already wanted to say something before Mr. Khan spoke, and I think the Chamber is one that rules on the proceedings and if the Chamber wants to make a statement, it makes it. We are now discussing merits, and it's not absolutely what we are supposed to be doing. We are supposed to hear evidence, and there is no issue now ex post on striking out questions. I would not be aware that that is done here. The Chamber, and I can speak of the Chamber because we have of course commented it, could not help noticing - and it has not been concealed - that between different Defences, there may be different views. There is a children's game with cards that in my language is called Black Peter. One is a card that you should not have in the end. So you try to turn it around and the one who in the end is stuck with it has lost. In this way, we perceive a certain tendency of different Defence teams to try to shift responsibility rather to another Defence team. That seems to us a natural development of things. It is inherent in the starting situation of this. So we cannot stop one party, one Defence from bringing its arguments which may to be the detriment of another Defence, and let the other Defence give her arguments. We must hear them all. And the fact that we hear them does not mean that we eat them and that we believe everything that is alleged. We are, Mr. Khan, aware and I think able of assessing the values of what Defence counsel in a different case brought forward as a theory, it's a theory of a Defence counsel and there are many such theories. So, I think we should not waste time and I think it's wasted in shifting arguments this way and that way, and we should go on with the examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you allow me just one sentence. General Petkovic's Defence will not absolutely shift responsibility for any combat action except combat activities undertaken by the Kaznic Kabojna [phoen] or the Convicts Battalion. This question was focused on contextualising Mr. Bandic's testimony and to test his credibility because Mr. Bandic was in French media, highlighted as a person who was active in the preparation of the Defence of Mr. Blaskic. I didn't want to dwell on this topic any further because the witness stated that he had no authority to discuss it further and this is why I concluded.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a technical question, everything is clear. There's nothing to add or subtract from these arguments. Everything has become clear, but I would like to point out that on page 19 it was not registered that Mr. Stojic said anything. If this could be rectified in this transcript. It's very important that we have it on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have a follow up question for you. After those questions that Ms. Nozica put to you. The event in Stupni Do occurred on the 27th of October 1993. I would like you to refresh your memory. I would be incapable of answering such a question. If somebody asked me, would I remember what happened 15 years ago I would not be able to, but I'm sure your memory is better than mine. On what date exactly was your service informed of this information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I've spent so much time to retrace all the steps and all the moments of that time, and believe me, this is extremely difficult, but my service, and personally apart from media coverage, apart from information placed by different media and different sources, my knowledge about that came from the interview with those two members of the Apostoli or the HVO unit which was active in the area of Vares and Stupni Do. My direct knowledge about that was generated maybe one month after the event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as you know, at the Defence Department or at the Ministry of Defence, whichever you like, this piece of news arrived one month later or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at that time when the action was underway around Vares, I was in Kiseljak together with General Petkovic. After that, I can't be specific as to the day, whether it was one day or two, we left and I cannot confirm with any degree of certainty when first information reached the Defence Department and the other institutions. I really do not know that. But I repeat, after several days, there was quite a lot of media coverage. It was very difficult to distinguish between propaganda and truth because no HVO institution could reach the site to collect any evidence or to perform any kind of investigation about this crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since you told us that you were in contact with General Petkovic, did you talk to him about this event? Did you discuss with him this event or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I reiterate, either that day or the following day or two days afterwards, we returned to Herzegovina, and we of course discussed the situation over there. We were the only persons in the vehicle. After return to Herzegovina for ten days, seven or ten days, I did not see the general, but after that we revisited the area of central Bosnia. I'm not sure about the date, but it was sometime around my birthday, 17th of November, and I believe that by the time we were back in the area of central Bosnia, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 17th of November. On the 17th of November you saw General Petkovic again. When you talked to him about these events how did he react? Was he surprised? Was he someone who did not understand what had happened? What was your feeling about this, if you remember, of course, if you can talk about it, otherwise if you don't just tell us and tell us that you don't remember which I can understand fully.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The only thing I can say, Your Honours, is that I remember that General Petkovic's comments reflected his complete supplies by those events. I know that we commented that there was an investigation going on. He was as surprised with the events up there as I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I believe that Mr. Coric's Defence counsel is ready. I shall therefore give her the floor. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. I don't know whether my binders have been distributed. I would like to ask the usher to give the witness the binder especially marked for the witness. There is a reason for that, the documents are sequenced in the sequence that I'm going to use them. I have my 15 minutes and Dr. Prlic's 15 minutes. I'm grateful for their magnanimus offer, which means I have 30 minutes in all. I now would like to start straightaway.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bandic, please take a look at the first three documents in my binder, then I will ask you a short question about all these three. These are P00803, P01457, and P02970. All three documents refer to the procedure of appointment of officers in military police. The first document is a consent to the proposal of the head of the military police administration on the appointment of an officer into the military police administration. It's the document sent by the Security Sector of the department for Defence dated 25th of November, 1992, signed by Mr. Lucic, assistant head. The second is dated 10th of February, 1993, signed by the head of the Defence Department, and it is a decision on the appointment in the Security Sector to the position of commander of a military police battalion. The third document is a proposal for an appointment of an officer into the military police administration, dated 26 of June, 1993. Document generated by the head of the police department Mr. Coric, sent to the head of the Defence Department. In the lower left corner there is a handwritten note. It seems to me that it reads, in agreement, and then the signatures of Mr. Lucic. I know that the Bench will inquire about that. And my question concerning all these three documents is, are you familiar with this procedure of appointment as is described in those documents, we have one decision, one request and one consent?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, Madam Counsellor, I have not seen these documents, but what you said is correct, and I know that this is Mr. Lucic's signature on the third document where it says, I agree and signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My colleague, Ms. Nozica, during the direct examination shows you a document of Mr. Ivica Lucic, it's the next document in your binder after these three, that is 2D00934. As you were giving your comments on this document, you said that this was an example of cooperation between the SIS and the military police administration, 2D00934 is the number of the document. I put it in the binder just to remind you what it is. It is the Mokronoge case and the killing of 9 civilians of Bosniak ethnicity, and it is a request for the military police to take action. You said to Ms. Nozica in response to her questions that you know that something was done and that the perpetrators were punished?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, Madam. If you allow me, Your Honours, this is a series of documents speaking of lawful appointments of certain officers. My position is that this is absolutely not controversial, that was the right way to proceed, the problem is with those who were not appointed in accordance with the rules or who did not work right. If we try to change them, that was simply impossible and unfortunately there were quite a few of such people.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm showing you the Mokronoge document, Mr. Bandic. Have you found it, 2D00934?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: I would like you to look at documents that will show what happened after that. P04143. Have you found it, that's the next document?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document from the Tomislavgrad police sent to the Military Prosecutor's Office in Livno. This is a criminal report against perpetrators unknown. There are nine injured parties here, and we see what this is about. Is that actually the case from Mokronoge, what Mr. Lucic wrote about in his request?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I'm not familiar with this document, but I think that that is precisely what it being discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I would like us to look at 5D02092. This is an entire series of documents, pertains to the Mokronoge case. My colleagues have cautioned me that the colleague does not reflect the name of the village properly, Mokronoge. It is an arrest warrant. It is dated the 13th of August, 1993. utterances.text: Could you please look at the next document, P--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, is this 2092? There seem to be two. Ivan Bakovic, nicknamed Ruda, member of the 2nd Guards Brigade of the Croatian army, 1st Battalion, 2 Company, currently based in Heliodrom barracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Were you aware of a fact that a military unit of the Croatian army, 2nd Company, 1st Battalion, of the 2nd guard was at the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I explain. Yesterday or the day before yesterday, you asked me about this person. I see from here that it is the HVO, so since I was not involved in this case, my first conclusion was on the basis of the last name which is a common one in that area. I believe that in due course, I will get an answer to this question of yours which will confirm what the witness said just now.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: We had a document, the interpreter did not catch the number, it was again an arrest warrant, and it was issued by the same organ and it has to do with two persons. Can we confirm that it's the same one, P0 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that counsel is speaking too fast. It is impossible to follow her at this pace. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] PD44 -- P04109. Or rather, 90. We've seen that. And now we've already moved on to the next document. P04190. P04190.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you are not only going too fast, you seem to be jumping, because you now say that we have seen the document P04190. Can you show me the trace of this in the transcript? Because I do not find it. I'm not aware that you have mentioned that document. This is -- we are repeating ourselves, but in fact this is really a problem. So please try to pull the brake, change into first gear, and allow us to follow and the interpreters. Thank you. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my question was recorded on page 29, line 21 through 23. However, unfortunately, the number of the document was not recorded. And I did say that yet again we have an arrest warrant, except that this time it pertains to two persons. However, I did not wish to dwell on that document because its content is practically the same like the previous PD ones so let us not waste time over that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask for a PD -- 5D04440. That is the next document. This document is a judgement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I am sorry, I want to go back to the previous document. Again both persons mentioned are mentioned with the reference HV. In the translation at least, it is said that this Guards Brigade, et cetera, is, I quote, "currently stationed at the Heliodrom Barracks." The word "stationed" in the English language, as I understand it, cannot refer to a single person who is incarcerated, but refers to a unit. Maybe this is again a problem of translation and it would be good if you could clarify. Thank you. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the document in the Croatian version it says "located at this moment." So it means that it pertains to one person who is a male. Let the interpreters correct me if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, could I ask, Mr. President, that we ask the interpreters or have the witness read the relevant text of both of the documents in the Croatian language so that we can get from the booth what the -- confirmation whether the translations we have are correct or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in this first document, which is --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Bandic, we were waiting for a ruling from the Trial Chamber first, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely. I gave him a sign to go ahead. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. So in this first document which is called "Arrest Warrant": "You are hereby ordered in relation to further operational work in the case of the killing of nine persons of Muslim ethnicity in Tomislav, to immediately bring into custody at the Ljubuski military remand prison the person by the name of Ivan Bakovic, also known as Ruda, member of the 2nd Guards Brigade of the Croatian army, 1st Battalion, 2nd company, currently located at the Heliodrom Barracks. After bringing the said person to the military remand prison Ljubuski, immediately notify the officer of the criminal investigations service in Ljubuski, Ivica Kraljevic. Your Honour, may I read the second document now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think it is not necessary because we can follow the wording in B/C/S and it's identical. I have a question to the interpreters of a grammatical character, the term here translated by station is "lotzivan," [phoen] and I wonder whether this form gives an indication as to whether this can refer to a unity or to an individual or to either a unity or an individual, if the interpreters could tell us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It is in the singular at any rate, so it can refer to a unit or an individual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, that's clear and precise.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave since it is my language after all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, I need to correct what has just been said in the transcript, because the interpreter said it refers to an individual, so can the interpreter confirm that the translation of the word in B/C/S refers to a unit and/or an individual?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: English booth repeats its original note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the booth says that it is a male masculine individual, and should be it a unit it would be feminine and singular?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: That would be correct for the word unit, "jebenica." [phoen] MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is what I said a few moments ago, and I am very sorry that Mr. Stringer doubted my professional integrity. I'm certainly not going to say before the Trial Chamber that there is something here in the Croatian language that is not there. 5D04440.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: This is a judgement of the district court in Zagreb. We see that it has to do with a person called Ivan Bakovic. After the wording "is guilty" we see that it has to do with something that happened in Mokronoge. What I would be interested in, witness, since you are a lawyer you will be in a position to answer my question, we have the number of the indictment referred to in the preamble, KT-465/93. Tell me, please, to the best of your knowledge, as a lawyer, this number, 93, does it denote the year when the indictment was issued?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I would like us to look at Mr. Bakovic's personal details. What is stated here was that he was born in Tomislavgrad. Do you see that particular detail?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: That would confirm what you said earlier on, that on the basis of the surname, you had assumed that he was from the area?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Bandic, do you know, and this was confirmed to us here by several witnesses so far, for example, Prosecution witness Mr. Biskic, then the Defence expert, the Stojic Defence expert, that many people who are originally from Bosnia-Herzegovina and who are Croats, at the beginning of the war of Croatia, in Croatia joined the units of the Croatian army, and then when the war started in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as volunteers they reported to HVO units and came to defend their people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Are you a ware of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. We are quite far away outside the scope of the direct examination, so I'd ask that counsel not ask leading questions on this topic. Thank you. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] All I would like to say is that my question follows on from the question raised by Their Honours during the examination-in-chief. Judge Antonetti asked yesterday already how this member of the Croatian army happened to find himself on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and two minutes ago we had a discussion about that, and I am showing the judgement here which unfortunately I don't have the time to read in extenso, but the Prosecutor has this, but anyway in the judgement it say that is it was indeed a volunteer. And my question does not go beyond the direct examination because the Judges themselves expanded the topic, went beyond the questions raised in chief, and the Prosecutor here also stepped outside the frameworks of the examination-in-chief. He said, I put it to you, witness, and then presented his case, we didn't all jump up and get to our feet, at least I did not because I know that he has the right to ask questions like that during a cross-examination, so I think that I am justified fully in asking this question now.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I have already described what the witnesses appearing this in courtroom said, I don't want to repeat that now, you heard the question correctly, do you agree with what those witness said and did you hear of cases like that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Madam, I agree with you absolutely. There were many people who came to the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina after the war began in those areas and this other case, Ivan Duvljak [phoen] although the surname suggests that he might be from the Duna [phoen] area, he is in fact from central Bosnia. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like now to move on to another area, so may we take the break now. After, you tell me how much more time I have so that I can organise my questions because there were a lot of interruptions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll take the break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The hearing resumes, Mr. Stringer you have a question to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, to you and to Your Honours. I just wanted to raise two points. First of all, I wanted to inform counsel for Mr. Coric that there was not any intention whatsoever to cast any doubt on her credibility or her integrity when I asked that the interpreters read the relevant parts of those documents. And if it was interpreted in that way, I regret that, but I wanted counsel to know that there was certainly no intention to impugn her integrity on that. I think -- there's a practice that we've done a number of times, just simply have the witness or someone read the passage and let the interpreters do their job, and that's all that I was proposing. Secondly, Mr. President, just as a way of a preview or a warning, and not to sort of anticipate news that might be coming from the Stojic team, but we are informed that over the evening in fact the witness's government, the Republic of Croatia, did give permission for the witness to testify about certain matters that were discussed yesterday on the condition that it be in closed session. And while on the one hand we are happy and gratified that we will be able to conduct our cross-examination as envisioned, all we have or I think all that there will be on this is simply a letter from the government of Croatia saying that he can testify on the condition that it's in closed session. Now, there has to be some greater showing to justify why closed session for this or any other witness is justified, and we've had any number of witnesses, representatives of other states, testify in closed session, I'll be the first to admit that. And -- but in every case there has to be a showing under Rule 75, 79 that closed session is appropriate and justified. And just based upon a blanket sort of letter like what we have, the showing is not being made. It's my intention, Mr. President, as I indicated yesterday, to ask the witness questions about the period of time when he was an intelligence agent for the Croatian information and security -- Security and Information Service, the HIS during 1997 and 1998 [Realtime transcript read in error "1987" "1988"] when he was attached to the Croatian embassy here in The Hague. And I'm going to be asking questions and I'm going to be putting it to the witness that part of his duties were to, in fact, obstruct and to sabotage the work of the Tribunal, and in particular the work of the Office of the Prosecutor, as regards to a couple of the Bosnian Croat cases that were taking place at the time. That might be embarrassing for the witness, and it might be embarrassing for the government of Croatia, but these are events that occurred over ten years ago now. And in any event, it's our view that these are not legitimate intelligence or national security issues, and therefore they are not appropriate issues to justify going into closed session. I just wanted alert the Trial Chamber and the Stojic Defence that that's our position -- or that will be our position and that we'll be asking the Trial Chamber to consider these issues in advance of the time we begin our cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm grateful to my learned friend's, I'm grateful for my learned friend's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second, Mr. Khan. I'd like to correct one thing, there's a mistake in the transcript, line 2, page 37, it is 1997 and 1998. Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm most grateful for my learned friend's indication. In my respectful submission, not only has he indicated his intention to object to the application for closed session, clearly given the amount of time he spent, he has raised his arguments now as to why the closed session that the Defence are conveying the request of the government of Croatia that the evidence be given in closed session, and I would ask that we respond to this issue now. Your Honour, whether or not my learned friend is happy with the response of the government of Croatia is, of course, an issue to be decided. Yesterday, he made no bones about the fact that he was going -- he was proposing on, behalf of the Prosecutor, to make the very drastic step of seeking to exclude the evidence of this witness in toto, and of course the Defence for Mr. Stojic say this is a relevant witness. Your Honours, overnight, at the request of the president and Your Honours, contact was made with the government of Croatia, and whilst, in my respectful submission, in accordance to the law and practice of this Tribunal, and Mr. President you, yourself, referenced General Wesley Clark, and there's numerous examples where the Trial Chamber in similar circumstances has limited and confined the ambit of cross-examination to witnesses -- to issues that have been raised in examination-in-chief. Notwithstanding all that jurisprudence that the government of Croatia said yes, fine, ask these questions, but the only caveat, notwithstanding the fact that these issues were not raised in examination-in-chief, notwithstanding the fact that these issues go out with the period of the indictment, notwithstanding the fact that these issues relate to the diplomatic functions of a state official, you may ask them consistent with the fair trial rights of the accused, the rights of the Prosecution to challenge the evidence. The only very modest, very mild condition that the government of Croatia has requested is this evidence be in closed session. It is bizarre, in my respectful submission, for the Prosecution firstly to object to that, and secondly to say Well, the accused, the witness, the witness may be embarrassed. The government he represents may be embarrassed. Your Honour, yesterday the witness said on the record, very clearly, even before we received any intimation from the government of Croatia, that he himself is completely content, completely content to talk about the matters that my learned friend intimated would be raised in cross-examination. So Your Honours, whether or not there is embarrassment in reality or whether or not my learned friend wishes there to be some kind of embarrassment which the witness, from what we've seen and the government of Croatia from the letter it has written, do not feel is a matter to be determined in due course. Your Honour, there is settled law, at this international criminal tribunal, while set -- predicated by Security Council Resolution 827 under chapter 7 of the Security Council, Powers and the Charter, is predicated on international law. And, Your Honour, the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations in the preambular paragraphs, makes it very clear that as part of the requirement for the committee of nations, diplomats do have certain privileges and immunities, and those privileges and immunities are not to be tossed aside as if they are of no consequence in the international legal order, but they have to be given the most anxious scrutiny and careful consideration, and that is notwithstanding the fact that this court has chapter 7 powers. Your Honours, the Appeals Chamber of this court has previously decided in the Blaskic subpoena case of 1997, and I quote: "The International Tribunal should not be unmindful," should not be unmindful, "of the legitimate date concerns related to national security." And they confirmed, in that case the Trial Chamber's position, suggesting that in-camera ex parte proceedings could be held in order to scrutinize the legitimacy of the state's concern. Now, Your Honours, for the life of me I'm at a loss. Despite the my learned friends's assertions of embarrassment and all this evidence that he think will demolish the credibility of this witness or embarrass the state concerned, I'm at a loss to see what Prosecution prejudice the Prosecution will suffer when they've been given every opportunity to challenge the evidence that we've called, to put any evidence to controvert the witness, and to so displace the legitimate state concerns when the area does not relate to the examination-in-chief of this witness. Your Honours, in the Milutinovic case, of the 11th of July, 2006, at paragraph 14, the Trial Chamber held that only brief statements were required. And Your Honours, when one is looking at the rules, one of course must look at Rule 79(a)(3) in which closed session can be ordered where it's interest of justice. It's my submission that ensuring state cooperation with this Tribunal, given the very modest restriction which is closed session, and Your Honours and the parties and the Prosecution can hear the evidence, that standard is made out on the face of the letter from the Croatian government, and we can hand that up in fact now, perhaps if the usher -- with the usher's assistance. Your Honour, the second matter -- just with your leave, is 75(a) of the rules, and in my respectful submission, both of those rules apply, and there is a good cause, good reason for the very mild restriction that Your Honours hear the evidence, the evidence can be heard. Otherwise, of course, what my learned friend is going to do is get back to his position of yesterday and say, Well, because he is prohibited, because of the condition of the Croatian government, because he is restricted because of an application he himself has made to examine in open session, the testimony, the evidence should be excluded. It seems to be rather a self-fulfilling attempt as a result to exclude evidence that the Defence say is relevant and probative to Your Honours determination of this matter. Your Honour, it's very clear that the privilege, both as a matter of Tribunal law, even United States law that my learned friend is familiar with, the United States v. Reynolds, makes it clear that the privilege attaches to the state, not the witness in the box. And for those reasons, it is my respectful submission that the closed session application should be granted as manifestly well-founded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Stringer, I'll ask you to reply very quickly because we are not going to spend the whole day on this. The Chamber will hand out its decision after the break as soon as we have all the elements necessary to hand out a decision, so please reply very quickly, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm very grateful for the opportunity to reply. I can invoke the UN charter or the Vienna Convention. I'm just looking at Rule 79, which lays out the grounds for which a Trial Chamber may order closed session, public order, morality, safety, security, non-disclosure of the identity of a victim or witness as provided in Rule 75; thirdly, protection of the interests of justice. The rule says that the Trial Chamber shall make public the reasons for its order. Now, the Trial Chamber doesn't have any information before it on which it can make a finding that closed session is justified under Rule 79. Mr. Khan's referred to national security. Croatia has not invoked national security. Croatia hasn't invoked anything other than a request or a condition that the testimony be in closed session. It doesn't say why. As I've said, I'm going to ask the witness about things that happened ten years ago. It's not clear why closed session is necessary. So that's my submission on that. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For Mr. Coric, you have 16 minutes left. Please proceed. We'll ask the witness to come into the courtroom. I'd forgotten him. I was so concerned by the Vienna Convention. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] While the witness is coming into the courtroom, I'll like to say to Mr. Stringer that I am sorry that there was a misunderstanding and I appreciate his efforts. We all seem to be a little nervous today so that might be the result of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, we apologise for having made you wait, but we had a procedural issue which will be settled later on today. You have the floor. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you've already been able to conclude from my examination, and you are a lawyer and well educated man occupying leading post, that I am dealing with the HVO authorities' attempts to uncover the perpetrators of crimes and that's something that I'll carry on with. Now, would you please look at document P01803, which is the next document in the binder. And it is a SIS document for the Rama Brigade dated the 4th of April, 1993. Would you look at the last page of that document, please. And because I have very little time I'm going to para-phrase what it says there in the third and fourth paragraph from the end, that the document describes various crimes and impermissible behaviour on the part of individuals and groups, and after that in the penultimate paragraph it says the following: The security service are in all the aforementioned cases, gathers certain data and registers individuals or notes down information on individuals so criminal charges can be brought against them if there is a case to answer. Tell me, please, the SIS Rama Brigade, acting in this way as described in the penultimate paragraph, was that in keeping with their authorisation and powers.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: May we now look at another set of documents which I think was shown by my learned friend Ms. Nozica, it is the next document, P02544. I first of all like to apologise to the witness because it's not the next document, it's the document after that. P02544 is the number, and we'll go back to the other one in due course. So P02544 is the document I'd like us to look at, and it is also a Rama Brigade SIS document dated the 28th of May, 1993. And it is an official note. The testimony of the witness whose name I won't mention, you can read it for yourself and bear it in mind, about an event that occurred on the 26th of May, 1993, in a place called Klck. Have you had a chance to look at the document and memorize the name of the victim? Now, let's go to the previous document, P02597 [Realtime transcript read in error "P02957"], which is a Rama Brigade SIS document again. And it is a report on events in the village of Klck and Krancici. And in the first paragraph, it says that it is about an event that took place on the 27th of May, and in the middle of that page we have the names of the victims, and the last name is the name that we saw in the other document. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: And it says further on in the document that after -- it is the sixth paragraph, after that the Rama Brigade SIS undertook further investigation and immediately arrested the suspects, or suspicious individuals, and then we have a list of their names. Would you retain the name of Jozo Glibo, please. And at the end of the text on the last page, last paragraph, it says that the detained Jozo Glibo, son of Mirko, and Zoran Petrovic are being questioned by the Rama Brigade SIS, and then it says what happened to the other three members which I'm not going to deal with. Now, let's go back to the first page of this document. My colleagues have told me that it says P02957 where it should be P02597. As I was saying, let's look at the beginning of the document, and the number up there, there's a number, and it is 03-02-40/93. Perhaps you could keep that page open when we move on the other document because it's the number that's important as far as I'm concerned. Now, would you look at the next document which is 20 -- 5D02069. Sir, you were an operative, and I see that it says at the top of the document that it says OA PAUK or spider, so I think that's Operation PAUK or spider. And it says, "General Data on the perpetrators of a Criminal Act," that's title. Can you explain to the Court what kind of document this is? What is this document, in fact.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, counsel, I don't know precisely who compiled this document, but I am aware of Operation PAUK which was introduced because of the many crimes that were taking place, and I think the year was the end of 1994, beginning of 1995. I'm not quite sure, but operation PAUK is something that is familiar to me and it was written about by the media.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, when general data like this are compiled, it is compiled in order to process a -- persons identified as the perpetrators of crimes; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, let's look at what it says in the written -- handwritten part of the document which is at the end. There's a handwritten note, and we can see there that we are dealing with events previously described in the Rama Brigade SIS document. We see the name Jozo Glibo mentioned, whom we saw earlier on, and down at the bottom it says, Rama the 1st of June, 1993, and then the number, 03-02-40/93. Now, can that be interpreted as being the number of the criminal report under which the document was filed?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this number, counsel, links up the note, official note, by SIS with the actual case. That would be my comment, because judging by the general information and general data, they wanted to draw attention to the other reports or notes where these -- this person was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, after having looked at those documents, I want to ask you whether they indicate the practical application of the SIS of the brigade's acts to do everything in their power to see that the perpetrators of crimes who have been identified at some point in time be taken to justice; am I right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Could I be told by the Registrar how much time I've got left, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please. It's very complicated because you have to reckon in the seconds as well. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as per our estimates, I may have some seven minutes still. I would need ten to 15, so if this will be a problem, I beg for another minute or two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have six minutes left. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, let's take a look at the next document. I'll be explaining the document, their contents, otherwise I will not be able to do it in time [as interpreted]. This is a document, P04177. This is another Rama Brigade SIS document which describes certain criminal offences, criminal activities, and as possible perpetrators troops, civilians, and some elements of the military police are being referred to. It concerns the events in the villages Podgradje, Lapsunj, Duge. Those are of interest to me. The report does not specify perpetrators' names, there's no mention of them. It doesn't cite any precise information about which military unit they belong to. My presumption is that the author of the report did not have such knowledge, otherwise he would have written them down. Can this be concluded? I'm late again to explain that those names were in the meantime detected, but had he known he would have placed them in this report?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this seems a logical explanation, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: The witness does not have this statement in the binder because it's a confidential statement by a witness, that's 3D0049 -- 429. This is a statement by a victim who was heard at this trial. She identifies the perpetrators, persons who molested her, Zoran Calic, and a person known as Mendzo, and this is what I state for the record. Now, let's take this document, 3D00422. This is a document that the witness does have in his binder. I will just say that in the statement that I mentioned, that person said that in the autumn in 1993, that she was visited by HVO military police, that she spoke about what had happened to her, and that no further mistreatment befell her after that. So we are discussing this 3D422. This is a document of the 1st Company of the 2nd Battalion of the military police of Livno. It is an official note, and in the introductory sentence it says, On ground of raping women of Muslim ethnicity, it is necessary to bring in the following persons, and then the previously mentioned gentlemen are named here. Ira Petrovic, aka Mendzo, Zoran Calic, et cetera, and some others. My question is very brief, does this document show that when those persons were finally detected and identified that they were prosecuted; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you a brief question without showing you any documents. My learned friend Nozica showed you a document concerning the situation at Neum. I don't know whether you remember. It's 2D00515.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: And that document described the situation where some people misintroducing themselves as heads of department of SIS personnel, then you were also shown the document P6908. This is document where a certain member of the Convicts Battalion Reuf Asanovic misintroduced himself as a member of the military police when we came to Heliodrom. Do you remember this document?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam counsel, it's possible that the document was mentioned, but I can't recall this name. I know that name Reuf Asanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: I just refer to those documents for the records. I do not have time. But the crux of my question is this. Have you heard of any cases where during the war, different criminals would offer false identity as members of certain military units or members of the military police or people holding certain functions or positions? Have you ever heard of such cases?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were such cases. You are right, Madam counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: And finally, I'm not sure whether these documents are under seal, I would like to seek my learned friend's Stringer's assistance to tell me whether they are, I have two documents, P03096, and P03988. These are Prozor prison warden's report. If they are under seal, I would be very grateful for their assistance to tell me whether they are or not. I can proceed without retrieving those documents. So when my learned friend Nozica showed you those two documents, you have them in your binder, from her examination I concluded that you were not familiar with the contents of those documents, that you used them to explain the ways that those were submitted, the reasons for them suppression, [as interpreted] et cetera, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are correct, Madam counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Can I conclude that you cannot confirm that the contents of those documents are credible and accurate if you are not familiar with the contents?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the contents. I wouldn't doubt their credibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know why I'm asking you? I'll be specific. In P03906, in the introductory paragraph, it is said that certain individuals --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel, we've checked, the two documents are confidential or under seal, so perhaps shouldn't read them publicly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Avoid reading it out and just state this document states this or that. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, but I'll have to deal with a detail, a very brief question, but I have a very important detail contained therein.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can move into private session in that case for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We've already made a public -- clear that if we do not use the time that were given by the bench, we are going -- giving it back. We explained it for principled reasons, and we would like to thank the ambassador and the Chamber. We have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. General Praljak will conduct the cross-examination, thank you very much, and I believe that you gave one hour to the Defence, and I believe that the remaining time is at the disposal of General Praljak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, except that it's a little bit more complicated than that since Mr. Pusic's Defence has given its time to the Chamber. I would have liked to have this time for myself to put some further questions. Now, what about General Praljak. You can only address military issues, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak has 18 minutes -- only military matters, yes, yes, absolutely. And events where General Praljak was involved directly or had immediate contact with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you have the floor. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I would just like it to note, if allowed, that this giving back of time, well, it can happen that examination-in-chief lasting three hours could refer only to one person, and if all the Defence teams were to give back the time, then that Defence team would be given only one-sixth of the one-and-a-half hours available. It would seem to me logical for the time to be owned by the Defence, and if the Defence team does not use it, then it should be transferred to the last remaining Defence team. I need at least half an hour. And Chamber can ask questions anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bandic.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right. Well, the Judges can put questions for the time that remains. And as soon as there is an opening provided, we put our questions because you are in charge of the time you have. Mr. Praljak, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Witness, on several occasions, you stated that the extent of chaos at the time and in that area was humongous; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Witness, sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption. Could we get a specification of what area, if there is a specific area that he is asking about, I think that would be helpful. What area of chaos he is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: I refer to the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina which was not occupied by the Republika Srpska army and the JNA and by the time not only of the signing of the Washington Agreement but also the Dayton Accords, but beyond that point up until today. But let's limit ourselves to the time before the Washington Agreement. Is it known to you that there was much chaos reigning in that area at the time.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bandic, please tell us whether in your work whenever you knew that there was a crime when you investigated, when records were kept in Prosecution or processing of such cases, have you ever instructed by anybody not to do it, to do it in a different way, were you obstructed in any way in attempts to investigate, record, and prosecute all forms of crime irrespective of the colour of skin, gender, ethnicity, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the basis of our work was that. You are right, Mr. Praljak, we had no limitations imposed on us by anybody in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did you have support under the circumstances prevailing to proceed in this manner?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did have support.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's discuss your role at the Main Staff at Grude. I do not want to contravene your opinion about that, but let's explore how things looked from the other side. So my question would be this, you said you were never formally appointed for that function?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Can you agree that I never seen your appointment document?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can agree that you've never seen it, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, witness, how can you affirm what someone else never had? Why do you say this, did you search all his papers, or what's the basis of this answer? Or do you simply say so because Mr. Praljak says so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have not seen this document, therefore I can leave the possibility open that Mr. Praljak had never seen it either. That would be my view of the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: All right. Your question is then -- your answer is not: I know he never had it, but I do not know whether he had it or not; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. I leave that possibility open.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that according to the establishment of the Main Staff there was no such position?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Praljak, I'm not sure. I cannot make any assertions whether that is the way things are according to establishment. However, I do claim that towards the end of 1993 and the beginning of 1994 in the Main Staff, there was an officer of the SIS and he was a member of the collegium.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: I can agree or disagree with you, but I would be interested in the 9th of November, that's what I'm talking about and you'll see why. Tell me, is it also correct that the commander of the Main Staff would have to agree to a proposal, according to the procedure that was in force, to establish who the representative of the SIS would be and the Main Staff, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the procedure. Your position is a logical one, but I'm not aware of the details. However, I do know that there was an officer in the Main Staff and, if you allow me, just a detail. In the beginning of 1994, since I knew Mr. Predrag --

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Bandic, up until the 9th of November, I'm talking about myself.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did you ever come to me, and if so when, did you ever come to me, did you say, Praljak, I don't have a piece of paper saying that, but I'm your assistant for SIS in the Main Staff. If you remember that, tell me what the date was?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember that any such thing ever happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, do you remember a single meeting that I held with my assistants that you attended yourself?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never attended such a meeting, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me one more thing from this last area. Do you remember any report that I received on my table that you had signed or somebody else at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall ever having signed such a report and having sent it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, since we have established that, let us move on. Do you agree with the fact, we've seen papers to that effect here, that forms of organisation were made in such a way so as to be as democratic as possible, like in democratic countries, but for many reasons this effort to make things happen the way they were on paper, that did not succeed?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right, Mr. Praljak. Objectively and subjectively some things simply could not be carried through.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let us leave chaos aside. Let us see what should have been done. For instance, you claimed that in brigades there were quite a few persons as if they had been SIS, that is to say security, but you had not confirmed them; right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: But, for instance, you state - you or your chief or your service - that person A in Brigade E was not appointed according to procedure. So then you send a piece of paper saying person A in Brigade E, we are dismissing you, but then the brigade commander opposes that. Tell me, at what meeting, at what collegium would this problem be presented; that is to say, you or your chief saying that the commander of the brigade is opposed to this? And then in relation to that, who would dismiss the brigade commander? For example, he is disobedient, he doesn't want to carry this through, who would replace the brigade commander? Do you know on the basis of military establishment, although you said that you do not know very much about military establishment?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, as far as this kind of dismissal is concerned, I really don't know. My knowledge of military establishment is very modest. As for the first part, you have correctly identified the problem. At these collegiums, I don't know at what collegium level this would be discussed, and in view of my own position, I did not attend a single one. It was impossible for me to be at these collegiums, so I really do not know at what levels this was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. All right. Remember the problem with the document concerning Zara Pavlovic and he was opposing something or whatever. I mean, the man is disobedient, so who is the person who is supposed to handcuff him and take him into custody, into prison?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The brigade police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Coric. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think it would be more logical to put a question before this question that was put by General Praljak. Who orders the arrest. If the witness could respond to that question before this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Witness. The procedure relating to arrests is quite complicated, since several people are associated and involved. The SIS drafts reports, the military police takes actions. Could you perhaps answer the question asked by Mr. Coric. According to you, who carries out the arrest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I absolutely understand the context. I absolutely understand the context of Mr. Coric's question. The commander commands that, and that is the brigade commander. However, in respect of Mr. Praljak's specific question, who brings him in, it's the military police.
