In the brigade in Capljina, the case of that man is one that I am very familiar with, and I know the man very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Orders is a word that is often used here. Orders given to a subordinate. You say that you are not an expert in military matters, but say in a brigade we have three battalions and every battalion has three companies, respectively. So we have nine, and then in the brigade there is one more, so then according to establishment there are ten SIS officials. Ten altogether. The commander of the brigade, can he tell these ten men, Look, this is the order, go to feature such and such, dig a trench this long, and fight there until I order you to do something different? Did he have the right to do that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My modest knowledge, Mr. Praljak, tells me that he was in a position to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. All right. We'll deal with that some other time. Now, P05249. It's an exhibit already. The 21st of September, 1993, is the date. Instructions for work to the SIS centre, Travnik, Vitez. Have you found the document?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: It says here some new changes were made, technical ones that is, in the organisational schematic. Seven centres for SIS were established, but please look at the last paragraph, the centre of the SIS is the highest organ of SIS in its territory, and then it says who is subordinated to who, and it says that there under the battalion commander, it's all explained very nicely here. Just look at this: Cooperation between the head of the operative zone and the commander. The commander of the operation zone is duty-bound to help the chief of SIS in the implementation of his duties and to cooperate with him. And then it says further on, that the chief of SIS is duty-bound to render assistance to the commander in the discharge of his duties, and on behalf of SIS, he attends meetings and the chief of the centre only if he is invited. Now, this is what is said, The chief of the SIS centre does not have the authority to issue orders to anyone outside the SIS. And then there's something that I'm particularly interested in, While discharging his duties, a SIS official has the right to ask for identification, SIS officials, and other citizens. And then, as far as crimes are concerned, belonging to the jurisdiction of military courts that are done in the course of official duty, then SIS officials can arrest a person and, without delay, take the said person to the investigative judge or the police. Then a SIS official can arrest --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could we please have the document displayed in e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: So this is something that is done in the course of official duty. Then this person has to be handed over to the investigative judge or the military police unit involved. Then we have this technical matter of two days in detention and whatever else, and then what you spoke of, persons who are supposed to be brought into custody can try to resist arrest, and physical force can be applied by SIS officials. And then the next page refers to that and that's what the document says, you've read it out. Mr. Bandic, isn't it clear that a SIS official is -- or, rather, the SIS centre is a person who is in charge, according to the law, to investigate and to apply force if necessary in order to bring persons into custody, suspects into custody?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That can be interpreted only partly in that way, Mr. Praljak. This is a special situation in central Bosnia. And this is one of the many efforts to establish a centre --

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: No, no, Mr. Bandic. Allow me to say this to you, just a moment, please. We've left chaos aside. We've said enough about that. Now, we are just looking at what this was. Wasn't this the ideal legal framework as to how things should have been done?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, if you'll allow me, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Go ahead, answer.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said for crimes that are prosecuted in the line of official duty, these are grave crimes. These are serious criminal offences, and the minimum sentence is three years. As a lawyer, I simply have to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Of course, and there are other sentences involved in the case of other crimes. Of course. Tell me, when you're in a particular area -- will you agree with me that I was out in the field a lot, that I spent a lot of my time out in the field, and that I know full well what the problems were? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fully agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Tell me, rape, arson, or something like that happens in an area where we were, and then someone comes to report that, or somehow one find out, the brigade commander find out, what does the brigade commander do at that point in time? What will he do?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Praljak, what was the duty of the brigade commander then was to issue an order to his security organs in the military police to establish whether a crime was committed involving all the facts that were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. But, for example, if the brigade commander is not there perhaps, if he is fighting somewhere else, he is running all over the place, he is on the front-line, then who is supposed to act in official terms?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the second part of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: This is not understandable. I think you started again. You started asking who was responsible and the answer was yes. That is not helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'll repeat, the brigade commander, if he found out, he called his SIS assistants, and he said, Now investigate that, you investigate that, call the military police. The military police of the brigade, we will agree, does not have the technical ability to handle this, it doesn't have its own crime investigation service; right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I really don't know. I really don't know whether they had a crime investigation service within the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. At any rate, my question is, if the brigade commander is not there, if he is out in the field, and one does find out about something that happened, a crime, the assistant commander for SIS, does he take over himself the investigation and everything else and order whatever is necessary to find out who the perpetrator was interpreter?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We can no longer hear the witness, too many microphones are on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, in the question put to you by Mr. Praljak, one element is missing and I'm going to mention that element. When the brigade commander isn't there, when he is absent, as far as you know isn't there another officer who can then perform the tasks as an acting commander for the brigade because the commander is on the front-line, on leave, sick, in Geneva, or God knows where? In the system you were familiar with, wasn't there always an officer who could replace the person who usually performs the task?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, absolutely that is the logic, that there is a person standing in for him. My response to Mr. Praljak's question as to whether the SIS officers and the military police could do that on their own, collect all of this, my answer was yes, I think they could have done that. As for the actual chain of command, it is certain that if the commander was absent for any reason, there had to be someone who would deputise for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. All right. Let us now look at document 2D00948. Now look at -- sorry, what was that? 2D00948. Yes, that's what's written here. Yes, yes, yes. That is a fine what is says on the screen. It is the 26th of June, 1993, Lucic writing to Colonel Blaskic. Obviously, there is some kind of misunderstanding involved, and he is explaining something to him. And look at the number 1, it says the role and tasks of the centre are defined in such and such a way. The centre is headed by a chief who is responsible to the chief of the SIS administration for his work and then it says further on, so there is no need for you to know what he is doing -- what they are doing or are you responsible for their work. Then number 2, the objective of establishing the centre is to improve the security situation in the area assigned to them for operations, to inform the administration about all types of organised crime within HVO units, et cetera. And then it says, I cannot enumerate all of this to you. It does say you are the most responsible person, the reference is to Blaskic, for the situation in the operative zone of central Bosnia, especially in terms of the establishment and activity of our units, but I believe that you do know that from the security point of view, we are responsible and how. And under number 4, it says that he sent a communication to the chief of the centre requesting him to consult Blaskic in the event of any activities which might have major consequences, et cetera. And that Blaskic's approval was necessary. Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Tell me now, please, an example. You are in the field somewhere on assignment, and you happen to come across an event, an occurrence, which is a crime, rape, et cetera. As a SIS officer with your ID card, would you undertake to arrest the perpetrators or would you take out a pistol and shoot, would you have the right to do that, and would you indeed resort to that kind of action?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that hypothetical situation, Mr. Praljak, that is what I would do. I would act that way. I did have the authority to do so. But luckily, I was never in a position of that kind. I never witnessed anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Allow me to say that unluckily I was never in a situation like that. Mr. Bandic, you said that the SIS did not start functioning, and I agree with that, of course. Now, tell me what did start functioning? What department, the military police, the Defence Department, the military setup, mobilisation, the financial sector, information, what did function down there? And if it's -- something did function, how far was it operational during the war and with all the dead and wounded and so on?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, that position of yours is true to a large extent, but we would need a lot of time and a lot of data and information to explain it. There were certain segments that were operational and did function, for example, within my service. There were parts which functioned very well. In other parts it functioned with great difficulty, so that it depended on the situation and the area in question and the time-period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, I'm told that you have gone beyond the time that was granted to you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] How much more time do I have?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have exceeded the time that was allocated to you by at least three minutes already. If you have one last question, please proceed, one to summarise, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, what can I say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Recapitulation, before I do that, did the SIS officers -- could they wear civilian clothes and military clothes in going about their business, when they were on assignment?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The possibility did exist for us to be in civilian clothes as well, yes, Mr. Praljak, but that was the exception, when there was a very highly sensitive situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, let's go back to document 2D00948 for a moment, please, and I've been told to ask whether you know whether the assistant head was Mr. Ivica Lucic, that that was the post he occupied?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, I am aware of that. That was his post at the time. And you see once again, it says assistant to head and chief of SIS. We see those terms used again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now my last question. Tell me, please, when -- well, I can't show you the documents for this, but I will mention it, P07035. A document referring to a particular event, so the document is an exhibit already. But anyway, expressions like "the investigation is underway" are used, "the perpetrators were unknown," and so on and so forth, "the whole case was handed over to the military police," and so on and so forth. And this brings me to the last question now. In the performance of your duty, whether it was the military police or a part of the army, a military man, did they ever refuse to provide with you assistance, or let me put it this way, any reported and recorded crime, was the maximum done to deal with it as much as resources allowed for, material, technical, and whatever, either in the Ministry of Defence, the Main Staff, whatever? Did you always have help in performing your duty to investigate every recorded crime, every single reported crime?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, yes, absolutely assistance was there but the question is was it sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, in the distribution of the crimes that we had over there, the people who perpetrated those crimes, for example --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you said it was your last question and now you are moving on to the next one and the following one. You need to be more disciplined, just as counsels are.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Praljak [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I do understand that, but now I come to my last question and then I'll finish there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: The distribution of those crimes. Was it nationally speaking different, were there different types of crimes, did you see as many crimes against Croats, arson, rape and so on, et cetera; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes the ethnicity wasn't important. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Bandic. Your Honour, Judge Antonetti, may I ask you once again, if the examination-in-chief is going to be conducted with one or two witnesses, then the time allotted to the Defence teams, if they don't use up their time, they should not return their time to the Court. They should return it to the Defence because the Defence is there to present their case because some teams might examine witnesses for three hours, and if you divide that up with six, and then you might have one Defence team have just 15 minutes. And then if you need to respond to allegations made against a particular person, then you would need to use that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we will see that amongst ourselves. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President on page 66, I believe it was line 11 and 12, there was a question by General Praljak, the gentleman had previously answered the question, but then General Praljak said but what -- were the resources sufficient for the gentlemen to conduct the various investigations that were required. And to that question, as I took it as a question -- as a follow-up question or clarification of the previous question, we did not receive an answer from the gentleman. So perhaps he could be asked that question to clarify whether he had sufficient resources at the time to cover all the investigations that were necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Witness, one of your answers was not recorded. Could you perhaps reply. General Praljak asked you whether you had all resources available to you to conduct your own investigations or to take action when necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have said several times already that the great problem was that we did not have the material, resources, and the manpower that we would wish to have had for us to be able to undertake all that work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had a question for you. I was wanting to put it to you yesterday. I saw this document which mentions the members of the SIS that could conduct their work in military uniform or in plain clothes, and General Praljak put the question to you again this morning. But I would like to address this from a different angle. Since in your department you collected information and you go and seek out this intelligence, this information, and in certain cases people are paid for this and people are prepared to give information if they are being paid. At the time in your department, did you have cash which would have enabled you to pay your informants?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, that was one of the ways in which the secret service worked. And I'm trying to recall just now. I'll not quite sure that we did have money earmarked for that kind of thing, but there were occasions where we did assist people, help people out through our sources. People who had helped us come by information or documents or things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A question of a technical nature you don't have to give us any names or specific examples. Did you have any informants who were working for the other side, either Serbs or Muslims, did you have your own informants on the in the other side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there were such instances, although that wasn't our primary job. It was the intelligence service that dealt with that mostly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for your answers. My colleague has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... under staffed. Now I would be interested to hear whether you have or Mr. Lucic has acted upon this and presented demands for strengthening your service to whomever? Was that done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, of course we endeavoured to both in the personnel sense and in the technical sense to strengthen the service, and Mr. Lucic certainly did request that for that purpose, but it was very difficult, please believe me when I say that, to find people who would come right up to the front-line in actual fact and deal with such sensitive work and dangerous work. It was a thankless task. And at the same time, we had another problem. We had problems in many other areas where even certain members of SIS would engage in unlawful actions. We had to deal with them too, just as we did our best to deal with all people within the HVO, and if I might be allowed to say, along with the difficult situation as it was, I have to say that I am personally very proud of the work we did with the very limited resources we had and limited manpower we had. I can say this, I was proud.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber will deliberate on the procedural issue. We shall come back in 20 minutes time hopefully then I shall read out the Trial Chamber's oral decision. So we'll be back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber will hand down its decision. Its oral decision. Considering the Prosecution's questions yesterday stating that he would like to ask the witnesses questions about his professional life, considering the objections submitted by Mr. Stojic's Defence team, considering the letter that we have received today, this letter comes from the Republic of Croatia in which it is stated that the republic of Croatia would like the witness's testimony to be held in closed session when certain aspects of his testimony are addressed. The Trial Chamber, after having noted the remarks of the parties in question, decides that the Prosecution will cross-examine the witness in open session when it comes to those questions that have been put to him during the examination-in-chief and during the cross-examination of the other Defence teams. However, the Trial Chamber orders closed session when the questions will relate to the professional career of the witness. Part of the witness's professional life that occurred after the period quoted in the indictment. Mr. Stringer, I'm sure you've understood. We are now in open session. If you address those questions that have already been addressed, but when you want to address specific matters we will have to move into closed session. Ms. Pinter, before I give to floor to Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would first of all complete the reasoning of our decision because I do not find it in the transcript, it is based on Rule 79 in the public interest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That is indeed right. My colleague is right in saying that the decision has been taken pursuant to Rule 79 of our rules. Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Since my client during his cross-examination was cut off, and for the record I believe that it would be important to ask another question concerning Exhibit 4D1654, and since the matter revolves around the issue of the Chamber's time, I would like to submit that the witness be asked about an event on the day 9th of November, 1993, where the witness personally escorted General Praljak on his travel to Zagreb pursuant to the aforementioned document 4D1654, or if you may let me to ask the question. It would be important in the light of all the presented evidence and since we have here a person who was present physically when General Praljak departed. It is relevant because of the claim --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Ms. Pinter. What document are you talking about? We've been given two documents, which document is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 4D1652. It is an article published in Globus magazine where Mr. Bandic's interview was published.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Pinter, it was for you and your client to put the question during your time. The Trial Chamber noted that General Praljak put a number of questions of different kinds of questions. Had it been extremely important to you, then you could have put the question. I don't see why we should get back to this issue now. Your position is recorded on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, but I still want to say that the Defence reckoned rightfully that it had one hour given to the Defence at large and not to individual Defence teams and expected to be able to ask this last crucial question to the witness. Since your decision is as it is, I cannot really deal with the reasonings, but I'm satisfied with it being included in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, your presidency. Let me explain the situation. Madam Pinter was maybe not here when I expressed my opinion. My opinion is of a general nature, I do not want to contribute to any shortening of time. It is up to the Chamber, if the Chamber wishes to give extra time to General Praljak's Defence or any other Defence time it is up to the Chamber. But given the circumstances in the [indiscernible] I may change my opinion entirely. Who knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I'm ready to continue. I oppose any other teams on the Defence side continuing cross-examination at this point. If I am able to finish early, I don't have a problem with someone getting the opportunity to tomorrow, but we are eating into my time and I'd like to start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have the floor since we have time constraints. Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not going to eat into the time of the prosecution, but I believe it would be fair for the witness to receive the letter sent by the Croatian government. He is the only one not being privy to it. I will ask the usher to show it to the witness. I believe that it is important that the witness knows what it's all about and to know what the expressed opinion there is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Bandic. You've got the letter there that we've all been talking about, and you have take the time to look it over. I can assure the Trial Chamber and you that when we get to the relevant part of your testimony I will ask to go into closed session before ask any questions related to your time as a agent with the Croatian intelligence service in the Hague during 1997 and 1998. Now, the Registrar has passed out binders, and, Mr. Bandic, there are three binders there that contain documents that I'm going to ask you to look at during your cross-examination. The first question I've got for you, it might be useful just to -- if you could put those on the floor, and then I can direct you to the specific binders that I'm going to -- that's okay. It's a lot of paper. My first question, and I want to take you back to July of 1993. Do you remember a man named Kasim Kahrimanovic he was a member of the ABiH 8th Mountain Brigade. You'd been attached to the logistics in Split. He was brought by the Croatian intelligence service on your request from Dubrovnik to Neum. He was then transferred to the prison camp at Dretelj where he was beaten to death on the 21st of September, 1993. Do you remember that incident?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Prosecutor, I've never heard of this name. It is not known to me and this case is not known to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could I ask you to look at Exhibit number P03630, which is in the first binder, the binder that's labelled number 1. 3630. And, yeah, you're going to have to find the document behind the tab that bears that number, 3630. It's toward the back, I think. Toward the back of the binder. Okay. Thank you. Now, this is an official note. At the end of it it's dated 22 July, 1993. It's an official note of some individuals with the military police administration, Capljina. And it says here that under item number 1 -- do you have the document now?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that this is the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Item number 1, the case of Kasim Kahrimanovic, who was transferred from Dubrovnik to Neum by the SIS of Croatia at the request of Tutic and Bandic, and from there to Dretelj at 1500 hours. Lucic was informed about the arrival of this person. He was placed in solitary confinement until 21 July, 1993. In the course of the day he was beaten up by persons who entered the barracks compound without authorisation, it continues on with their names. It says that Boskovic did not take part in the beating, but military policemen did. The said man died at about 2000 hours was buried in Pocitelj during the night. Do you remember this gentleman, this man, Kasim Kahrimanovic, who according to this appears to have been brought to Dretelj at your request?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Prosecutor, I do not recall at all this case, I do not recall the name of the person who suffered, and I cannot recall having absolutely any connection with this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Where it says here that Lucic was informed about the arrival of this person, do you know whether that would be a reference to your superior Mr. Ivica Lucic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I'm not sure and I cannot claim that this refers to Mr. Lucic, because there a possibility that this would be him, but there is also a possibility of somebody else being referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Is it true that members of the military police administration did report to Mr. Lucic or to yourself, that there was reporting and sharing of information as between these two branches of the security arm of the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Prosecutor, I repeat, I really do not know anything about this case. I've never heard of this name. It is not known to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, at the time of this event in July of 1993, Mr. Bandic, you were, if I understand correctly, chief SIS officer, you were attached to or you were linked to the Main Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, my position, as you've seen from different documents, carried different labels or titles, but I'm not sure whether during that time I was in the area of Herzegovina or whether I was in central Bosnia, I don't recall where exactly I was at the time. But I reiterate, I do not know anything about this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you about your position at this time, and we'll talk about the variety of labels that apply to your position. I'm asking you whether at this point in time if you recall, were you linked to or attached to the Main Staff as opposed to the SIS administration?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, on several occasions, I've said that from autumn 1992 I was attached, so to speak, in a manner to the Main Staff in the sense that I was escorting Mr. Petkovic on many occasions. I've never seen an official document whereby I was appointed as assistant for SIS at the Main Staff. I really do not know specifically what my function was, whether I was in the SIS administration or formally was a part of the Main Staff, and I do not know physically whether I was out in the field, whether I was at Mostar or maybe at Citluk.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: 22 July, 1993, is just about the time where there was a change in the command at the Main Staff. Do you recall that on or about the 24th of July, 1993, Slobodan Praljak became the commander of the Main Staff of the HVO replacing Milivoj Petkovic who up until that time had been the Chief of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Esteemed Mr. Prosecutor, throughout my time there, I was never sure who of them was the commander and who was the chief. I remember meeting, now late Stanko Matic on the premises. I'm trying to recall the name of another person who was either assistant commander or vice-Chief of the Main Staff. I was never sure what exactly their titles were, what ranks they held, whether general, major, major general, or general colonel, or whatever the rank was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Between general Praljak and General Petkovic, you can't say who was in a superior position at this -- at around this period of time in July of 1993; is that correct? You don't know?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really do not know who at the time was chief and who was a commander. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, you've indicated that you were regardless of what title or position you may have had or not had on paper, that sort of in a de facto way your role was to accompany General Petkovic as his security officer, is that a correct way to put it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's partly accurate, Mr. Prosecutor. I've just explained because of the nature of the job, the circumstances prevailing, and when there was a need for General Petkovic to go to central Bosnia, I would be the person escorting him back.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, based on the position that you held and the functions you carried out, did you have the authority to have people like Mr. Kahrimanovic brought in from outside and placed in one of the HVO camps? Did you possess that authority?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, as I understand it and I reiterate, I know nothing about this case. I do not have such powers or authorities to command anybody, particularly in such a case as this, is what is to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You say you don't remember this case then. Do I understand correctly that you don't know -- you've never subsequently became aware of the beating death of Mr. Kahrimanovic at the Dretelj camp? You never heard about that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reiterate, I've never heard about this case, unfortunately, so such a drastic case simply has not reached me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then do you deny the possibility, do you exclude the possibility that you could be the Bandic person referred to here on whose request Mr. Kahrimanovic was brought to the Dretelj camp?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecutor, I cannot bring myself in connection with this event in any way and the person concerned. I don't know whether anybody noticed -- mentioned me in any context, but I personally know for sure that I don't know anything about this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, turning to page 2 of this document, Mr. Bandic, there's a reference toward the end where these two military police people, Mr. Kraljevic and Mr. Buntic say as follows, they say: "Beatings of prisoners by members of the military police with the knowledge and in the presence of the commanders are regular in Dretelj prison." Now, as a high level person within the SIS, if I can put it that way, directly linked to and working for General Petkovic, did you at any time during the summer of 1993 become aware of beatings of prisoners that were being carried out by HVO personnel such as the military police?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Prosecutor, again, I repeat, I know nothing of this case or of such cases, particularly at the time while I was together with Mr. Petkovic. We did not discuss these matters. If we had not been informed about them, then we could not have known about them. I don't know now anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you ever go to the Dretelj camp, the Gabela camp, Ljubuski military prison, Heliodrom military prison? Did you ever personally go into any of those HVO facilities during 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Prosecutor, during 1992 and 1993, on several occasions I visited those places.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell me to the best of your recollection when you visited each those facilities?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. I'd like to mention the Prosecutor said "visited" and the witness did not say "visits." He said that he had been there, so he is being put words into his mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question. Maybe there was an interpretation issue there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm asking you, Mr. Bandic, whether during -- I asked you, actually, whether during 1993 - we can limit ourselves to 1993 - did you personally go inside any of the HVO camps at Dretelj, Gabela, Ljubuski, or Heliodrom? And if so, to the best of your recollection, when did you go into each of those?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Prosecutor, I said I was there. I confirm that I went to Heliodrom two or three times, and once I think it was the Grabovina prison, the entrance to Capljina, during the Neum case. Other collection centres and prisons, with respect to them I cannot recall ever visiting any of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when you went to the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Prosecutor, I cannot recall, but there must be written traces, there must have been a note on an interview I conducted or written record of the warden about my visit because I could not have visited those without prior approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And this anticipates an issue that we'll talk more about later, but then your purpose in going to the Heliodrom was to conduct interviews of detainees who were of significance, of interest?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, Prosecutor. There were two or three instances. I could almost recall the persons I spoke to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And this was one of the functions of the SIS administration, that being to gather information and intelligence from detainees; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That was one of the duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, if I could take you back to page 1 of this exhibit, which is P03630. At the very beginning it says: "A series of undesirable things have occurred following the political decision to detain Muslims in the municipalities of Stolac, Capljina, and Neum, and to set up prisons in Dretelj and Gabela." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know what political decision that is referring to?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Prosecutor, I really do not know which political decision is being referred to, and I don't know whether such a political decision has ever been taken. This is not known to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Is it true that the setting up of prisons at Dretelj and Gabela, that those facilities fell under the jurisdiction, if you will, of the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Respected Mr. Prosecutor, this is not known to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know which arm or entity within the HVO structures then was responsible for the camps at Dretelj and Gabela?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not known to me which structure that was, Mr. Prosecutor. There was talk about this that attempts were made to determine who was responsible for which camp or military prisons or collection centres, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, to the extent that the SIS went to the camps to conduct its interviews, would it be fair to say that on that limited point, the SIS was in contact with HVO military police in order to gain the permissions necessary to go into the camps and conduct the interviews?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, Mr. Prosecutor, that is your question, duty of members of the SIS, if they wanted to conduct interviews, was to address the person in charge of the respective institution, be it the military investigation prison, or otherwise. That means to whoever was the commander or warden of that institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you said that you were not aware of or you don't know about a political decision to detain all the Muslims in these municipalities. Mr. Bandic, were you aware, nonetheless, that on the ground throughout these municipalities during the months of July and August of 1993, in fact the Muslim male population was arrested and placed in the camps by the HVO? Were you aware that that was taking place?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Prosecutor, it was known to me because unfortunately that was an event which has caused quite a lot of damage to both the Croatian and Muslim peoples because then conflict broke out and we've discussed the matters of events at Mostar and Stolac and the brigades which had numerous Muslim members or Bosniak members. That is the period I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And in that operation, the operation of rounding up the Muslim population, the male population, is it true that the SIS in fact played a role in identifying prisoners and locating the prisoners from the municipalities into the various camps?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, Esteemed Prosecutor, I know that there were different cases when people were brought into custody, either on account of military assessments or security related assessments. The security service tried to follow these developments, collect information about it, and forward it, as far as such developments are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know whether SIS personnel in the field actually coordinated with the SIS administration and the Department of Defence in actually determining where these people would be sent once they were rounded up and arrested? Was there coordination on an institutional level between the SIS and other bodies?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I'm not aware of the extent to which it existed. Of course, members of the security service and the military police tried to follow all of what was happening. Also, in centres, people tried to gather information about this as much as possible and then to notify their superiors of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next document I'd like you to go to -- Mr. President, yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, before we move on to the next document, I would like to come back to this specific document, and particularly its first paragraph where I see that two members of the military police, first of all relate all the unfortunate events that took place, deaths, people being beaten up, et cetera. However, what I'm particularly interested in is the following: I see that there's two policemen referred to consequences of political decisions as it were. That's exactly what it says here. As far as you know, were there within the HVO administration or within other bodies, were there elements that would have enabled you within the SIS to become aware of the facts that some people seemed to be in disagreement with what was happening? Because when we read this document, we see that those two members of the military police say that this is all a consequence of a political decision. So at SIS level, were you aware or made aware, I wouldn't say of people challenging, but have you seen documents that were criticising certainly a given action?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. President, in this case, I really don't know what the two policemen mean when they say in respect of political decisions. I really don't know what kind of political decisions these were and at what level these decisions were made. I really don't know. I don't know about that personally, and I also don't know about that being known at the administration, that anything like that had reached the administration, so I really don't know what decisions these could have been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But the question I'm asking you, sir, relates to another document which I don't have here. I'm quoting it from memory, but there was also a member of the military police who drafted a report where ethnic cleansing is mentioned, ethnic cleansing carried out by Tuta's men, and this document also stemmed from the military police. So if I put the pieces together of the various documents that we have seen, I'm led to conclude that the military police was reporting events at the very least and that's precisely what I'd like to know. Within the SIS, were you made aware of facts stemming from reports made by the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In part, yes, Your Honour. There was such information too, but in this specific case this you referred to, if what is being said that ethnic cleansing is taking place, either by a regular or irregular unit or a part that is out of control, these were free interpretations, highly so, and what was meant by that. What I can say to you that at that time in June, July, August, in the territory of Herzegovina, there were large scale conflicts, or, rather, major problems between the HVO and the BiH Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The floor is -- you have the floor, Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Bandic, you can set aside that binder. The next exhibit is in the little binder, the smaller one, yes. And it is P10890. 10890. And what this is, sir, is last week we went and we found your resume on the website of the Croatian government, and that's what this is, and I've got a couple of questions about your CV. And what I want to do is go to the second page of it, and I'm actually going to start at the bottom of it and work upwards. My first question is when I looked at this, I saw that one of your hobbies is karate and that you are a karate master. And I know that one of our accused Mr. Coric is also a karate master. And looking into this further, I had the impression or the understanding that you and Mr. Coric have some form of close family relation, I'm not sure whether you were the best man at his wedding or perhaps the Godfather of one of his children; is that correct.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Prosecutor, if that is relevant, of course I can confirm my very close friendly relations with Mr. Coric, that date back to a time long before the war and, inter alia, Mr. Coric was my trainer. As for our kum relations, if that is necessary, I can explain that too. His wife was Godmother to my children, as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Now, moving upwards on this page, I want to ask you a few questions about the time when you were at the, as indicated here, Ministry of Interior Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that's indicated for the period of 1987 to 1992. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And if I understand correctly, this is a period of time when you were with the Yugoslav state security office, that is the security apparatus or a security apparatus of the former Yugoslavia; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, Esteemed Prosecutor. That was my third job and it had to do with the secret service of the then state.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think we're at the point where we're going to need to go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In open session, the hearing stands adjourned. We shall reconvene tomorrow morning at 9.00. I wish you all a pleasant afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
